title: There and Back Again: My Journey with Gallagher's Article of the Week Assignment
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This article chronicles Stuart Jr.'s adoption and progressive adaptation of Kelly Gallagher's Article of the Week assignment, a weekly routine in which students read complex informational texts, annotate purposefully, and respond in writing. Stuart traces his journey through five phases: initial implementation using Gallagher's materials, creating original articles in that format, layering in scaffolds such as rubrics, Reading for Meaning statements, and a They Say/I Say template, recognizing those scaffolds had grown unwieldy, and ultimately returning to the original simplicity of Gallagher's elegant design. The piece functions as both a practitioner's memoir and a practical guide, offering concrete strategies for hooking reluctant readers, modeling annotation, running Friday discussions, and grading the assignment with intention. A core principle runs throughout: that the AoW, done consistently over 40-plus iterations per year, addresses reading, writing, argumentation, and time management in a single elegant weekly structure.
points: The AoW assignment addresses reading, writing, argumentative thinking, and time management in one weekly routine that compounds over 40-plus iterations per school year — a scope no single lesson or unit can match.
Increasing student motivation to engage with a text functionally lowers its felt complexity, making hook design the first and most important AoW implementation move.
Teaching annotation purposefully — oriented toward the written response students will produce — is more productive than margin-filling for its own sake.
Friday discussion and pop-up debate around the AoW text adds public speaking practice and draws in students who engaged minimally with the reading itself.
Scaffold accumulation can transform a streamlined assignment into an unwieldy packet; distributing scaffolds once as reference tools rather than embedding them weekly preserves the design's power.
quotes: Before the Common Core were a twinkle in David Coleman's eye, Kelly introduced an assignment into his classroom called article of the week. In the assignment, students read complex informational texts and responded to them in writing. That writing was nearly always a blend of the explanatory and argumentative modes, and it often culminated with a discussion of the issues in the text.

One way I addressed this problem [of students not having the background knowledge required for being multi-textual readers] in my classroom was by adding a weekly reading task I call 'The Article-of-the-Week.' These are real-world writings taken straight from news stories, essays, editorials, blogs, and speeches. I cull them from newspapers, magazines, and websites.

When motivation to read a text increases, the complexity of the text decreases. Tattoo this on your arm if you have to because it's one of the key truths we must cling to if we're to help our students read things they might not choose to read on their own.

Just as I try to schedule fifteen minutes each Monday for teaching/modeling/getting students started with the article of the week, I also try to schedule fifteen minutes each Friday for a quick, graded discussion and/or debate. Even with large classes, it's possible to get every kid talking and getting some public speaking practice around the text in fifteen minutes — the pop-up debate strategy is a key routine for making this happen.

I can still remember a student named Caleb who struggled getting the written part of articles of the week done until he discovered that annotations could serve as a starting point for his written response. As is so often the case, Caleb's epiphany became my epiphany, and the seeds for this idea of teaching kids purposeful annotation were planted in my skull.
